International **CONFIDENTIAL** 3-Year Copper Forecast - August 2009 ### **1. Introduction & Executive Summary** ##### **1.1 Introduction** In the previous edition of our 3-Year Copper Forecast, GFMS noted that due to lower than expected copper production figures and a change of sentiment towards the global economy, had boosted copper prices and set the backdrop for further gains going forward, despite the market remaining in surplus for the year. Three months down the line, our projections have proven to be correct, but too cautious, as prices have recently shot through a series of year-to-date highs. The official LME quote set a new high for the year of $6,419/tonne in mid August, a two-fold increase from the year-lows of January. We have often argued that the copper price rally seen over the last few months has largely been the product of speculative activity on the metal, in line with the rest of the base metals complex. Nevertheless, we note that the exceptional position of copper, enjoying the most positive fundamentals within the complex, has also contributed to this. In the short-term given the extreme rally so far this year, the downside risks seem to exceed the upside ones and we would expect a correction to take place before the end of the summer period (in line with the wider base metals complex). This seems yet more probable, given our understanding that investor purchases over the last few weeks present a significant overhang in the market. In addition to the nature of the recent price rise, this understanding that copper is overbought is confirmed by the limited publicly available data on copper investment, as well as anecdotal evidence. As noted later in this chapter, CFTC reports on speculative positions in Comex futures on copper as well as the LME futures open interest data are both pointing to a notable rise in long positions over the last few weeks. Elsewhere, the consensus view in the market confirms investments in commodities having exploded recently. These conditions, make the prospect of liquidations likely in our view. Despite a correction being probable in the very short-term, we envisage its magnitude to be limited. Figure 1.1

Later in the year and particularly in the last quarter, as global consumption begins to recover and the aforementioned deficit conditions start approaching, we expect investors will once again be attract

ed to base metals and that copper will be one of the main beneficiaries of this move. Although our projections see a market still in oversupply, we expect prices will trend upwards for much of the quarter, pushing prices comfortably back over the $6,000/tonne boundary, and we would not be surprised if they exceeded $6,500/ tonne. ##### **1.2 Market Background** Before discussing our projections on copper supply and demand as well as our expectations on prices, it is worth providing a brief overview of the conditions that have affected the market recently. Although copper prices were among the last of the base metals to peak at $8,985/tonne on July 3 2008, the performance since then has been remarkably similar to the rest of the sector. As noted earlier this yearto-date and particularly from March onwards, prices have recovered to current levels around $6,000. As we have discussed in our previous research, the main theme in the copper market has been the battle between tight supply and the weak demand environment. The 2008 production statistics illustrate that the former remains a feature of the market, with examples being the grade problems keeping Chilean output low and African Copper-belt production once again failing to live up to potential. Moving to demand, despite much talk of “green shoots”, with the exception of China, demand remains weak across all the key markets for copper, although it is now clear that the low point is behind most of them. A key condition that differentiates copper from other base metals is that it is the only one for which LME inventories have actually declined on a net basis this year-to-date. Following increases in the last quarter of 2008, stocks continued growing in January and February this year, peaking at just under 550,000 tonnes. Since then, they kept to a declining trajectory through to mid-July, largely as a result of exceptionally high flows into China. Regarding the growth in Chinese imports, it is worth noting that this has accounted for much of the growth in apparent consumption in the country. As we discussed in the previous edition of this report, we would expect that part of the metal that went into the country over the first six months of the year reflects additions to unreported stocks, which could well have offset the year-to-date declines in LME inventories. It should be noted that when discussing first-half consumption figures in China, we do not attempt to strip out the stock

-build from ‘real’ consumption in the country, as meaningful estimates on the split are difficult to generate, given the opacity of the market, and as we expect them to be offset by inventory declines later in the year. Nevertheless, the low level of LME inventories (at endJuly they represented a little over one week’s Western World consumption), is undoubtedly supportive of higher prices. As discussed later in this chapter, even taking into account our forecast surpluses for 2009, the stock build is not excessive from a historical stand point, which is another factor to make us positive about the long-term prospects for the metal. ##### **1.3 Economic Assumptions** As noted in the introduction, over the last few months there has been a notable improvement in sentiment towards the outlook of the global economy. A detailed overview of the latest key indicators GFMS monitors is provided in Chapter 2. As noted in that chapter, most of these have been improving over the last few months, suggesting that the downturn has most probably bottomed out. We expect that in the short to medium term the improvement (from a low base) will continue to one extent or another under all three scenarios. Specifically these scenarios see the following: **Base case:** (with a 40% probability outcome). Despite improvements in the second half, global GDP is forecast to decline at the margin in real terms in 2009. The bulk of the decline is forecast to come from mature economies, although, within the BRICs, Russia and Brazil are also expected to suffer negative growth. Global growth is forecast at -1.8%. As the recovery that commences late in the year gathers momentum in 2010, global GDP growth

moves into positive territory and reaches 1.7%, close to our projections featured in the previous edition of this forecast. Growth continues in the last two years of the forecast period, at 2.7% and 3.0% respectively. **Scenario B:** (with a 35% probability outcome). Under this scenario, the ‘real’ recovery begins immediately after the Summer, pushing growth in the last quarter comfortably into positive territory and resulting in the global figure amounting to 0.8%. China is instrumental in this, as growth in that country is forecast at 8.5%, although a recovery in the US and the EU27 countries also provide noteworthy contributions, as the real declines in both amount to just 1%. Thereafter, the global economy enters a period of strong growth, although we note that the rates seen during 2004-2007 are not matched. Growth in the last three years of the forecast period is forecast at 3.1%, 3.7% and 4.0% respectively. **Scenario C:** (with a 25% probability outcome). Under our most pessimistic (and in our view least likely) scenario, the current buoyancy in the markets proves unjustified, as the third and last quarter results disappoint. Global GDP declines by 2.3% in real terms in the year overall. The recovery that starts in 2010 fails to impress, with the Chinese economy only managing growth of 6.6% in the year, resulting in a global figure of just 0.7%. In the process, the greenback has more than lost its gains of the first quarter of the year. Concerns over a period of strong inflation, in the aftermath of a policy of quantitative easing in the US, as well as a heightened risk appetite impacting the safe haven appeal of the US dollar have fuelled this move. We expect the dollar to continue to weaken moderately during much of 2010 as the economy tentatively improves. However, after that, as the global economy starts to return to more normal c

onditions we expect the dollar to strengthen from its low starting point. This is based on the exchange rate being pulled back towards purchasing power parity, as the US economy recovers a little sooner than that of the Eurozone. GFMS has often argued that the tone of base metals investment is frequently governed by that of the wider commodities complex. This is due to the fact that, with the exception of a small minority of niche institutional players, the bulk of investor activity in base metals is the outcome of investor activity in commodity basket products and primarily those linked to one of the main commodity indices (such as the GSCI and Dow Jones AIG). The above-mentioned anecdotal evidence confirms this has indeed been the case recently. Figure 1.9 provides further support to this. The graph plots rolling 20-day correlation coefficient between log-returns in the copper price and the Dow-Jones AIG Commodity Index as well as the GSCI. The horizontal lines in the chart at the boundaries outside which the correlation coefficients would be statistically significant. Based on the graph, we note that the link between copper and other commodity prices has been strengthening over the last few weeks. ##### **1.5 The Funds** After a disappointing last quarter of 2008 and first few months of this year, when liquidations were followed by investors largely keeping away from commodity markets or even shorting them at the margin, interest in the long-side has returned in recent months. Anecdotal information and the little publicly available data available confirm that commodities investments grew notably over the second quarter of the year and through to the present time. As we have noted in our work in the past, precisely quantifying the magnitude and nature of investor activity in copper is an almost impossible feat. Nevertheless, daily observations of non-commercial and non-reportable positions in Comex futures, included in CFTC reports are thought to provide a proxy to speculative activity on the exchange. Figure 1.10 below features weekly on the aforementioned CFTC long positions on Comex copper futures as well as the daily open interest for LME futures, both of which are in line with evidence of strong investor buying over the last few weeks. In addition to the above, the data also confirms the existence of a noteworthy overhang in the market. As noted in the introductory section, liquidations from this overhang will in our view be the catalyst for a correction, before investors return on the buy-side and, at least in part, fuel a rally in the last quarter. Looking further ahead, it is our view that investors will on balance be a positive force for copper prices over the 2010-2012 period. Details of how we expect their activity to affect prices under the three scenarios in particular are provided in the outlook section of this chapter. A general point regarding investment demand for copper recently and going forward relates to the types of investors involved in the market. During the bull market through to the middle of last year, the bulk of activity in base metals, and by implication copper, came from speculative investors such as hedge funds, with a short to medium term investment horizon. Although interest from longer-term players such as sovereign funds and pension funds in commodities did exist, it comprised a smaller part of the overall market. This is gradually changing, with a growing number of such players making allocations in commodity baskets, often including copper. The possible implication of this change is that a growing and more or less inert (as such investors don’t tend to move into and out of markets very frequently) long position is being built on the metal, which could provide protection to prices against speculative liquidations going forward. ##### **1.6 Consumption** The contention presented in our last Quarterly Report was that global copper demand in 2009 would fall by almost as much as it did in 2008. According to the latest data by the ICSG, which estimates demand fell by 2.9% y-o-y up to April, combined with our revised estimates for the rest of the year, we believe a scenario not too far off will prevail. GFMS believes global copper consumption will register a 0.1% increase to reach 18.023m tonnes by the end of this year, much of it being owed to significant growth in the BRICs, in particular China. In 2010, we expect to see a 7.7% advancement to 19.407m tonnes, of course from a low base. This growth will then be followed by growth of 4.6% in 2011 and 4.5% in 2012. In this period, we expect demand in the BRICs not only in terms of percentage but also volume to outpace that in the mature economies. Overall, GFMS is forecasting global copper consumption to reach 21.215m tonnes by 2012. Figure 1.9

Plagued by structural constraints and technical difficulties in key operations and, to a far lesser extent, the handful of price-related cutbacks announced late last year and in the first few months of 2009, global mine production is forecast to register a modest decline of 1.6%. The situation is largely unchanged from our last Quarterly report in this respect. Despite a number of projects being pushed back by a year or so over our forecast period, we expect a strong recovery in production over 201012. Production next year is expected to rise 4.6%, with growth of 7.3% and 6.9% in 2011 and 2012, respectively. We expect African refined output to grow significantly over the forecast period, with major expansions taking place in the Democratic Republic of Congo and Zambia. Asia will also see significant growth in production. The largest producing region, the Americas, sees its growth emulate primarily from the south of the continent. Chile, fuelled by expanding capacity and increasing utilisation rates (partly related with Escondida overcoming some of the technical difficulties it has suffered), will provide much of the growth. ##### **1.8 Market Outlook** ###### **Base Case Scenario** As noted earlier, the strong Chinese consumption coupled with expectations for a recovery outside of the country to commence late in the year have led us to revise our projections for demand to show marginal growth for the full year in 2009. Our forecasts for production, in contrast, remain more or less unchanged. The implication of the above is that GFMS’ forecast for the market surplus in 2009 is now lower than in our May Quarterly Report when we forecast a surplus of 441,000 tonnes. The 245,000 tonne surplus forecast for the year does not, in our view, necessarily contradict the decline in LME inventories registered this year-to-date. As noted previously, we understand that over the f

irst seven months, much of that material found its way into unreported inventories, largely in China. As these inventories begin to weigh on the local market, we would expect imports into the local market to fall, resulting in LME stocks beginning to once again rise. Nevertheless, as the trends in supply and demand are clearly suggestive of a noteworthy improvement thereafter, this is expected to be short lived, with funds and user front-running the swing to deficit we expect will materialise in 2010, setting a positive trend for the price from Q4 this year. At that stage, we would not be surprised to see prices topping $6,500/tonne and generating a Q4 average of $6,000/tonne, resulting in a full-year figure of $4,900/tonne. Inevitably, the focus of the market in late July/early August has been on the impact of investment funds. However, as we have discussed there has been support from the underlying fundamentals. The tightness stems from the shortage of concentrate. GFMS forecasts that global concentrate production will decline by 1.6% this year following

no growth in 2008.  Latest developments in spot treatment charges reflect this situation, and the decline in spot treatment charges is sending “bullish” long term signals to the copper market.  In the key Chinese market spot TC/RCs in early August have fallen to $20/tonne (2c/lb) from $40/tonne (4c/lb) in June and $90/tonne (9c/lb) at the beginning of the year.  The benchmark price for this year was $75/tonne (7.5c/lb). 

A strong recovery in consumption coupled by slower mine production (and by implication refined production) growth are the architects of the 88,000 tonne deficit we forecast for 2010.  In addition to the direct impact of the improvement of the fundamentals on prices, the swing of the market to deficit (as well as the improvements in the wider commodities complex) is also expected to trigger additional investor interest in the metal, which will further boost prices.  Copper cash prices are forecast to top $7,500/tonne, averaging $6,500/tonne over the year. 

The deficit is expected to persist throughout the rest of the forecast period, and its magnitude in fact grows in 2011 and 2012, to 121,000 tonnes and 176,000 tonnes respectively.  It should be noted that not all of the inventory reduction will take place on the LME as we believe that there has been a build of unreported inventories within China. ###### **Mine Production** 

Over the last few years, copper mine production has tended to be the most problematic among base metals. ###### **Oceania** 

**Oceania** as a region has lost share of global mine production over the last eight years, dropping from 7.8% in 2000 to 6.8% in 2008.  Output in the continent has moved sideways over the period, as a result of declining capacity in a number of operations offsetting much of the limited increases noted elsewhere. Regarding the latter, these have tended to comprise small-scale operations, typically less than 50,000 tpy.  Examples include Newcrest’s Ridgeway operation (started up 2002, due to close in 2011 and be replaced by Ridgeway Deeps), Strait Resources’ Tritton mine (opened in 2004, currently only at 24,000 tpy) and the Lady Annie project (at around 19,000 tpy) in Australia. 

Going forward, there are a number of larger projects set to come on line within our current forecast window, which will help bolster the region’s production.  The biggest one is Prominent Hill, which commenced production in February 2009 (see Table 4.5) and is expected to reach full capacity of 104,000 tpy by 2010. By implication, after suffering a 7.6% decline in this year, Oceania’s mine production will grow by an annual avera

ge 4.5% in the following three years through to 2012, a rate which although modest far exceeds the average since 2000 (0.2% annually through to 2008). ###### **Asia** 

The relatively modest growth in Asian refined production is forecast to continue over the course of the 2009-2012 period (at least compared to expected capacity growth), and is in large measure due to the continent’s dependence on imported concentrate. The region will account for at least 40% of the global refined total over the forecast period.  Coupled with SXEW production accounting for an increasing portion of global production, this suggests that, over the forecast period, a decreasing portion of global mine output will be available for Asian countries to import and refine into cathode. 

Having accounted for 48.6% of Asian output last year, we are forecasting **China’s** refined production share, after growing by between 6-8% post 2010, to increase to 52.7% by 2012.  The most notable additions are likely to come from Tongling’s Jinlong eventually 350,000 tpy plant, Shandong Fenxiang’s 400,000 tpy plant, which will be achieved in 2012 and the Yunnan’s 200,000 tpy Baoding refinery.
